items.transcript: [music] >> Hi, welcome to another video. So, over the last couple of videos we've been talking a lot about Deep Seek V4 Flash. First, the 0731 update that massively upgraded its agent capabilities, and then how to use it cheaply through command code. But there was always one thing missing in the Deep Seek story, and that was a proper first-party coding agent. Anthropic has Claude Code, OpenAI has Codex, Google has their thing. And Deep Seek users have always had to plug the API into third-party tools like Kline, Open Code, Kilo, or Command Code, and hope the harness plays nice with the model. Well, that gap is now basically closed because Deep Seek's official API docs now have a dedicated integration page for a tool called ReasonX. And this is the most official kind of integration Deep Seek has ever had for a coding agent. So, let's talk about what it is, how it works, and how you can set it up. But before we do that, let me tell you about today's sponsor, Outskill. So, a few weeks ago Anthropic did something that no AI company wants to do. They pulled one of their own models off the internet, worldwide overnight. The model was Claude Fable 5. Was it too powerful? Then 2 and 1/2 weeks later the ban was lifted, and Fable 5 came right back online, more capable than before. Now, a model doesn't get banned and then reinstated unless it actually matters. That's exactly the kind of power sitting inside Claude right now. And to be honest, most people are barely using 1% of it. That's why Outskill is running a free two-day AI Claude hackathon this weekend from 10:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. EST. It's a full deep dive into Claude models and 10 plus other AI tools. It's usually paid, but the first 1,000 people who sign up through my link get in with a 100% discount. Over 10 million people around the world have already gone through this training. In 2 days, you'll run deep research with Claude, build artifacts and dashboards, put together full presentations, and set up connectors that automate the boring stuff, even your job search. You'll also get hands-on with Claude Code, build your own AI agents, and generate AI visuals and videos. And you're being mentored by actual leaders from Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Nvidia. If you attend, you also unlock bonuses worth over $5,100. Then, that includes 50 secret cloud codes, a complete AI prompt library, and a personalized AI toolkit builder. If you're even a little serious about cloud, this isn't one to skip. Grab your free seat through the link in the description and the pinned comment. Now, back to the video. So, first, what is Reasonix? Reasonix is a DeepSeek native coding agent that runs in the terminal. And the key phrase here is DeepSeek native. This is not another multi-provider tool where DeepSeek is just one entry in a long model drop-down. Reasonix talks directly to api.deepseek.com without a translation shim in between. No OpenAI compatibility layer, no adapter, no proxy. The whole agent is engineered around how DeepSeek's API actually behaves. Now, let me be precise about the official part, because I want to be honest here. Reasonix itself is not made by DeepSeek. It's an open-source project maintained by S-engine on GitHub. It's MIT licensed, and it's community developed with around 4.6 thousand stars at the moment. The repo itself doesn't claim any official DeepSeek endorsement. But, and this is the important part, DeepSeek has now put Reasonix directly into their official API documentation with its own quick start page under agent integrations. And DeepSeek does not do this for random tools. Their docs are pretty minimal in general. So, when the company itself is documenting how to use this specific agent with their API, complete with setup instructions and commands, that is the closest thing to an official DeepSeek coding agent that has ever existed. It's kind of like how it went with GLM and their coding plans, where specific harnesses got blessed by the lab itself. The lab picking your tool is the endorsement. And when you look at how Reasonix is built, you can see why DeepSeek picked it, because the whole design lines up perfectly with how DeepSeek's API works. The readme describes three main pillars. The first one is a cash first loop. The entire agent loop is organized to keep the prompt prefix byte stable across turns. So, DeepSeek's prefix caching keeps hitting over and over. We talked about this in the command code video. In agentic coding, most of your tokens are the agent rereading the same context in a loop. And on DeepSeek, cash hits are dramatically cheaper. ReasonX takes this to the extreme. They even publish a real case study of a long running session with 435 million input tokens at a 99.82% cash hit rate, which cost around $12 instead of the roughly $61 it would have cost without caching. So, the tagline is literally prefix cash stability. Leave it running. That is a very DeepSeek way to design an agent. The second pillar is tool call repair. When the model produces a slightly malformed tool call, ReasonX repairs it instead of just failing the turn. And if you remember, this is the exact same thing Command Code highlighted when they integrated V4-0731. Open models sometimes fumble tool calls, and a harness that fixes them on the fly gets way more reliable agentic behavior out of the same model. And the third pillar is cost control. By default, ReasonX runs on DeepSeek V4-Flash, which after the 0731 update is honestly a really strong default. And then when you hit something genuinely hard, you just type {slash}pro and it uses DeepSeek V4-Pro next turn only and then drops back to flash. If you want pro for the whole session, you run {slash}preset max. So, the expensive model is one command away, but you're not paying pro prices for every trivial file edit. This flash first approach is exactly the workflow I recommended in the last video, except here it's built directly into the agent. Now, let's set it up because this is genuinely one of the easiest setups I've seen. First, you need node. The official DeepSeek docs say node 20.10 higher, while the GitHub readme asks for node 22. So, just grab a recent node version and you're fine. On Windows, you'll also want Git for Windows. Then, get your API key from the Deepseek platform. And then, you literally just go to your project folder and run NPX ReasonX code. That's it. No global install needed, no environment variables. The first run opens a built-in configuration wizard that asks for your API key and stores it in your home folder in that ReasonX/config.json. If you prefer a proper install, you can also run npm install -g ReasonX and then just run ReasonX code in your project. There's also ReasonX chat for plain conversation without any file system access. ReasonX run with a task in quotes for one-shot commands and ReasonX update to upgrade itself. And inside a session, /help shows you the full command reference. Now, feature-wise, this thing is surprisingly complete for a community project. Edits are done as search and replace proposals that you review and approve with /apply. So, the agent isn't silently rewriting your files. There's a plan mode for thinking before doing. There are persistent per workspace sessions, so you can leave a project and come back to where you left off. You get MCP support over STDO, SSE, and HTTP, so you can hook in external tools. There's a skill system where you can create markdown-based skills with /skill new and they can run inline or as sub-agents. There's a memory system with user, project feedback, and reference memory types. There are lifecycle hooks for shell commands and workspace-scoped permissions. It even has some stuff that big tools don't have. There's built-in web search through Mojik, SearXNG, or Metaso. There's semantic code indexing that can run through a local Ollama model or any OpenAI compatible endpoint. There's a pre-release desktop client built on Tauri with multi-tab support. And in a very Chinese ecosystem move, there's a QQ messaging integration. So, you can literally connect a session with /QQ Connect and talk to your coding agent remotely through QQ. That one made me smile, to be honest. One thing I do want to be up front about is what ReasonX is not. The project has an explicit non-goals list. It is DeepSeek only by design. No multi-provider support, no IDE integration, no air-gapped mode. They position this as a feature, not a limitation, because coupling to one back end is exactly what lets them do the byte stable caching and the tool call repair so aggressively. But, it does mean this is not a Claude code replacement for everyone. If you want one tool that hops between 10 providers, this is not it. This is for people who have decided that DeepSeek is their daily driver and want the harness that squeezes the most out of it. So, how does this fit into the bigger picture? Well, to me, this is DeepSeek quietly assembling the full stack. First, the 0731 update turned V4 Flash into a legit agentic model. Then, they adapted it for the Responses API and CodeX. And now, their official docs are pointing people to a DeepSeek native agent with Flash as the default and pro one command away. And with the official DeepSeek V4 Pro release supposedly coming ASAP, ReasonX is sitting right there as the tool that's already wired for it with the /pro command ready to go. So, what's the verdict? If you ask me, if you're using DeepSeek models as your main driver, ReasonX is now the most aligned harness you can get, and the fact that it's featured in DeepSeek's own API docs means the model is very likely being tuned and tested against this kind of loop going forward. It's free. It's MIT licensed. It's a 2-minute setup with NPX. And the cash-first design directly translates into real money saved. I'd still say try it next to Command Code if you want plans and credits instead of paying the API directly. But, as a pure DeepSeek setup, this is the one to watch now. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like [music] this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, [music] give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
